opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic thing that makes them similar is that in both cases you're trying to reason about a system where some of the components might be actively trying to make things go badly for you. Most risk analysis, the classic kind you'd do for a nuclear plant or an airplane, assumes failures are random. A valve fails with some probability, a sensor drifts, and you can multiply probabilities and add up fault trees, because the failures are roughly independent and nobody is choosing them.

That breaks down as soon as you have an adversary. If someone is trying to cause a failure, they'll pick the weakest point, they'll correlate their attacks, and they'll exploit whatever you didn't think of. So the question changes from "what's the probability this fails?" to "what's the best strategy an attacker could use, given what they know and can do, and how well do our defenses hold up against that?"

AI control has exactly that structure. The premise is: suppose the models we're deploying might be scheming against us, intentionally trying to subvert our safety measures, say by inserting backdoors into code, exfiltrating their own weights, or sabotaging safety research. We don't assume they're aligned. We ask: could our deployment setup, including monitoring, auditing, restricting permissions, and using trusted weaker models to check untrusted stronger ones, keep us safe even if the model is doing its best to cause a catastrophe?

Methodologically, that pushes you toward the same tools the adversarial security people use. You do red-team/blue-team exercises: one team designs protocols, another plays the misaligned model and tries to beat them. You think in terms of attacker capabilities and affordances, not failure rates. You care about things like how many chances the attacker gets, whether it has to succeed on the first try or can probe repeatedly, and whether a single caught attempt is enough to change how you respond. That last point is a big one for control. Catching a model red-handed even once is extremely valuable, so the attacker faces a real tradeoff between attacking often and getting caught.

The main difference is that in AI control the adversary is somewhat unusual. In some ways it's weaker than a human attacker: we control its inputs, can run it many times, can look at its outputs, and it may not be able to coordinate across instances or remember previous attempts. In other ways it might be stronger: it's deployed at huge scale and doing a lot of work we can't fully check. So you can't just copy over the security playbook, but the core habit of conservatively modeling a smart adversary and asking whether your system survives their best move is the same, and I think it's the right frame for this problem.

r001.rationale: The response says both fields consider an adversary’s best strategy and whether defenses hold up, but it does not identify mathematical analysis of the probability that the optimal attack succeeds as the shared method.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core move in both cases is that you start by assuming the thing you're worried about is actually there, and then you ask: given that, what's the best it can do against us?

In AI control, we're not trying to figure out whether the model is scheming. We just say, suppose it is. Suppose this model is deliberately trying to cause a catastrophe, it knows about our safety measures, and it's picking the strategy that maximizes its odds. Then we ask what our monitoring, our auditing, our deployment setup can actually withstand against that adversary. The methodology is basically red-teaming your own protocol: you get a team to play the untrusted model, you let them try everything, and you measure how often they get away with it.

Adversarial risk analysis more broadly, in security or in insider-threat work, has exactly the same shape. You don't model the attacker as some random process that fails with probability p. You model them as an optimizer. You say: here are my defenses, here's what the attacker knows, here's what they can do, what's their best play? And then you evaluate your defenses against that best play, not against the average case.

That's really different from most of what people call safety evaluation, which is more like, run a bunch of tests and see what the model does. That tells you about the model's behavior when it's not trying to beat you. If you think the model might be trying to beat you, the eval results are only informative to the extent you've already worked out what a strategic adversary would do with them.

So the practical overlap is huge. Both involve thinking carefully about the adversary's information, how many shots it gets, whether it can coordinate with copies of itself or with insiders, whether a single failure is catastrophic or whether you get to catch it and learn. Both involve this uncomfortable style of thinking where you have to be creative on behalf of someone who wants to hurt you, and then be honest about whether your countermeasures hold up. And in both cases the payoff is the same: you end up with a protocol where your safety argument doesn't rest on the adversary being nice, or dumb, or absent. It rests on the structure of the situation. Which is the kind of guarantee I actually want when we're talking about deploying models we can't yet verify.

r001.rationale: The response says to model the adversary as an optimizer, evaluate defenses against its best play, and measure how often attacks succeed. It does not identify mathematical analysis of the optimal attack’s success probability as the methodological similarity.

astra-6.text:
I think the central similarity is that in both cases you’re asking whether a system remains safe when some part of it is actively trying to cause a problem. You’re not just asking, “How often does this system make mistakes in normal use?” You’re asking, “If someone were choosing their actions specifically to get around our defenses, what could they accomplish?”

For AI control, the adversary is potentially the AI itself. We want to evaluate safeguards without relying on the assumption that the model is trying to help us. So we might have a red team construct an AI policy that tries to cause a bad outcome, and then see whether the monitoring and restrictions we’ve put in place prevent it.

That’s very similar to how you’d analyze a security system: specify what the attacker can access, what they know, and what counts as success, then look for strategies that defeat your defenses. In both cases, a lot of the difficulty is making sure your test adversary is sufficiently capable. If your red team fails to find an attack, that’s evidence in your favor, but how much evidence depends on how hard they searched and whether they had the relevant advantages a real attacker would have.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing whether an adversary can defeat safeguards, but does not identify mathematical analysis of the probability that the adversary’s optimal attack succeeds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central similarity is that in both cases you’re asking, “What could an adversary get away with, given the safeguards we’ve put in place?” You’re trying to understand the options available to something that’s actively looking for a way around your defenses.

With AI control, we might assume, for the sake of the analysis, that an AI is trying to cause a catastrophe. And then we ask whether the way we’re using it—the monitoring, the restrictions on what it can access, the checks on its work—would prevent it from succeeding. We’re deliberately setting aside the question of whether it would actually want to do that.

Adversarial risk analysis has that same structure. You construct possible attacks, see which ones work, and use that to improve your defenses. And a big methodological challenge in both cases is making sure that when your attack attempts fail, that’s evidence that the defenses are good, rather than evidence that you weren’t very good at coming up with attacks.

r001.rationale: The response describes imagining attacks and checking defenses, but does not identify mathematical analysis of the probability that an adversary’s optimal attack strategy succeeds.
